stem: From an investor's point of view the expected return E[R] on an investment is the _____; from the borrowing firm's point of view the very same number is its cost of capital.
options: realized holding period return
coupon rate printed on the bond
required rate of return
accounting return on book equity
explanation: Lenders and investors supply the capital and need E[R] as compensation for the risk they take; the borrower must pay that same rate. One rate, two views: it is the investor's required return and the firm's cost of capital. Realized returns and coupon rates are different things.

stem: Investors in listed pipeline companies of similar risk currently require 6.1% per annum. Bow River Pipelines wants to raise money for a new line that has the same risk as those companies. For this financing decision, the 6.1% is Bow River's:
options: internal rate of return on the new line
accounting return on book equity
cost of capital for projects of that risk
dividend payout ratio
explanation: The rate investors demand for a given level of risk is what the borrower must pay to attract capital, so it is the cost of capital for projects of that risk. An IRR is what a specific project earns; it would be compared with the 6.1%, not equal to it.

stem: Which statement correctly separates a required return from a realized return?
options: A required return is what was actually earned last year; a realized return is what investors hope to earn next year.
A required return is always just the risk-free rate; a realized return is the risk-free rate plus a risk premium.
They are the same number measured at different dates, so over any period the two must be equal to each other.
A required return is the forward-looking reward investors need for the risk; a realized return is what was actually earned.
explanation: Required returns look forward and are tied to risk; realized returns are outcomes. A stock can realize 30% or −10% in a year while investors' required return stays near 9%.

stem: Why should two projects of similar risk be discounted at similar rates?
options: Because projects of similar risk must always have identical cash flows in every future year.
Because investors can choose either, so each must offer a similar expected return for its risk.
Because the discount rate is fixed by contract with the firm's lenders for all projects.
Because the NPV of a project does not depend on which discount rate is used.
explanation: All investments of similar risk should offer similar returns (L06 s45). If one offered more for the same risk, investors would bid its price up until the returns converged.

stem: Aspen Foods considers a new snack line. Shareholders of listed snack-food companies with the same risk require 9.5% per annum. Aspen's best estimate of the new line's expected return is 8.2% per annum. What does this tell Aspen?
options: The line is attractive because 8.2% is well above the risk-free rate, so it earns a premium.
8.2% is below the 9.5% required for this risk, so investors could do better elsewhere; reject the line.
The line is attractive because any positive expected return adds value for shareholders.
The 8.2% should replace 9.5% as the firm's cost of capital, since it is the project's own figure.
explanation: A project must earn at least the return investors require for its risk. Beating the risk-free rate is not enough; the benchmark is the 9.5% cost of capital for similar-risk businesses.

stem: Which statement is NOT part of the link between investing and financing?
options: The lender's required return is the borrower's cost of financing.
Investments of similar risk should offer similar returns.
A firm may pick any discount rate it likes for a project, whatever its risk.
E[R] is the required rate of return to the investor and the cost of capital to the firm.
explanation: The cost of capital is set by what investors can earn on other investments of the same risk, not by management's preference. Choosing it freely would let a firm accept bad projects by picking a low rate.

stem: Prairie Gate Rail has just paid an annual dividend of $1.90 per share. Dividends are expected to grow at 4% per year indefinitely and the shares sell for $38.00. Investors' required return, which is also the firm's cost of equity, is what percent per annum?

errors.label: Used D0 instead of D1
errors.explain: The dividend was just paid, so next year's dividend is D1 = D0(1 + g) = $1.976.

errors.label: Left out the growth rate
errors.explain: Required return = dividend yield + capital gain yield; the dividend yield alone is only part of it.

errors.label: Subtracted g from the yield
errors.explain: R = D1/P0 + g. The capital gain yield (g) is added to the dividend yield, not subtracted.

explanation: R = D1/P0 + g: the 9.20% that shareholders require is what Prairie Gate Rail must earn on equity-financed projects of this risk, i.e. its cost of equity.

stem: Foothills Brewing's shares carry about average stock-market risk. The T-bill rate is 2.8% per annum and investors require an equity risk premium of 5.9% per annum for average market risk. What return do investors require on Foothills' shares, in % per annum?

errors.label: Used the premium as the whole required return
errors.explain: The premium is only the extra reward for risk; the investor also needs the risk-free return as the base.

errors.label: Used only the risk-free rate
errors.explain: T-bills are risk free. A risky stock must offer the risk-free rate plus a premium.

explanation: Required return = risk-free rate + risk premium. This build-up is the idea behind the cost of capital: base reward for waiting plus extra reward for bearing risk.

stem: The cost of capital is the return a company actually earned on its investments last year.
options: True
False
explanation: False. The cost of capital is the forward-looking return investors require for the risk of the funds they provide. A firm's past earned return is a realized outcome and may be above or below it.

stem: Which expression builds the required return on a risky asset?
options: E[R] = R_F − risk premium
E[R] = risk premium ÷ R_F
E[R] = σ × R_F
E[R] = R_F + risk premium
explanation: The required return is the risk-free return plus compensation for risk: E[R] = R_F + risk premium, so the premium is E[R] − R_F.

stem: Why does a riskier borrower typically have to pay a higher interest rate than a safer one?
options: Because the risk-free rate is higher for risky borrowers.
Because riskier borrowers always earn higher profits, which they share with lenders.
Because risk-averse lenders need compensation for the extra risk the riskier borrower carries.
Because lenders in Canada are required to charge more to firms with a higher standard deviation.
explanation: Investors and lenders are risk averse, so they want compensation for higher risk. That compensation is the extra interest (risk premium) the borrower pays; the risk-free rate is the same for everyone.

stem: An investor says, "I will not buy this stock unless it offers me at least 10% per annum for the risk I am taking." That 10% is the investor's:
options: required rate of return
realized holding period return
standard deviation of returns
dividend payout ratio
explanation: The minimum expected return an investor accepts for a given risk is the required rate of return. It is the same number the firm sees as its cost of capital.

stem: The risk premium on an asset is:
options: the extra expected return over R_F that compensates for risk, E[R] − R_F
the total expected return of the risky asset, including the risk-free part
the standard deviation of the asset's returns, which measures its risk
the expected return on the whole stock market portfolio
explanation: Risk premium = E[R] − R_F, also called the excess return. It measures only the reward above the risk-free rate, not the whole return and not the risk itself.

stem: Chris will move money from a 3% GIC into a stock fund only if the fund's expected return beats 3% by enough to pay him for the extra risk. Chris is:
options: neutral toward risk
risk seeking
risk free
risk averse
explanation: A risk-averse investor wants compensation (a premium) for taking more risk. An investor who is neutral toward risk would need no extra return; a risk-seeking investor would even accept less.

stem: Pat holds a speculative stock whose expected return is below the T-bill rate because she enjoys the gamble. In the professor's classification Pat is:
options: risk averse
neutral toward risk
risk seeking
diversified
explanation: A risk-seeking investor is willing to give up expected return to take on risk, so a lower expected return is acceptable. A risk-averse investor would never accept less than the risk-free rate for more risk.

stem: Which statement best separates risk aversion from risk avoidance?
options: Risk-averse investors refuse to hold any risky asset.
Risk-averse investors require the same return for every level of risk.
Risk-averse investors prefer the asset with the higher standard deviation when expected returns are equal.
Risk-averse investors do take risk, but only when they are compensated for it.
explanation: The professor's point: risk aversion does NOT mean people do not take on risk. It means they want compensation, so riskier assets must offer a risk premium.

stem: Government T-bills currently pay 2.6% per annum and the stock market is expected to return 9.4% per annum. What is the equity risk premium, in % per annum?

errors.label: Reported the market return, not the excess
errors.explain: The premium is the return above the risk-free rate; subtract R_F.

errors.label: Subtracted in the wrong order
errors.explain: A premium for bearing risk is E[R] − R_F, so it is positive when the risky asset is expected to do better.

errors.label: Added the risk-free rate
errors.explain: The premium is a difference, not a sum.

explanation: Equity risk premium = 9.4% − 2.6% = 6.8% per annum: the extra reward investors expect for holding stocks instead of T-bills.

stem: Over five years Okanagan Orchards' shares returned 18%, −7%, 24%, 11% and 9%. Treasury bills averaged 3.9% per annum over the same five years. What was the stock's average historical risk premium, in % per annum?

steps.label: Average risk premium = average return − average T-bill return

errors.label: Did not subtract the T-bill average
errors.explain: That is the stock's average return, not its premium over the risk-free rate.

errors.label: Divided the sum by N − 1 when averaging
errors.explain: The mean divides by N. The N − 1 divisor belongs only in the sample variance.

explanation: The historical premium is the average stock return minus the average T-bill return: 11.0% − 3.9% = 7.1% per annum.

stem: A Canadian equity fund returned 14%, −9% and 22% over three consecutive years. The one-year T-bill returned 3.0%, 3.4% and 4.1% in those same years. What was the fund's average risk premium over the three years, in % per annum?
solution: Average risk premium = 9.00% − 3.50% = 5.50% per annum (same as averaging the three yearly premiums 11.0, −12.4, 17.9)

errors.label: Subtracted only the latest T-bill return
errors.explain: The risk-free benchmark must be the average over the same three years, not the last year's rate.

errors.label: Reported the fund's average return
errors.explain: That ignores the risk-free return the investor could have earned.

explanation: Average the fund returns, average the T-bill returns over the same years, then subtract: 9.00% − 3.50% = 5.50% per annum.

stem: Analysts expect the stock market to return 10.2% per annum and estimate the equity risk premium at 7.1% per annum. What risk-free rate is implied, in % per annum?
solution: Risk premium = E[R] − R_F, so R_F = E[R] − risk premium

errors.label: Added the premium to the market return
errors.explain: Rearranging premium = E[R] − R_F gives R_F = E[R] − premium; adding goes the wrong way.

errors.label: Reported the premium as the risk-free rate
errors.explain: The premium is the excess over R_F; it is not R_F itself.

explanation: Rearranging risk premium = E[R] − R_F: R_F = 10.2% − 7.1% = 3.1% per annum.

stem: Stock Q is expected to return 12.35% per annum and the risk-free rate is 3.15% per annum. What is Stock Q's risk premium?
explanation: Risk premium = E[R] − R_F = 12.35% − 3.15% = 9.20%. Adding the two gives 15.50%; reversing the order gives −9.20%; subtracting 0.0315 from 12.35 (a percent-decimal mix) gives 12.32%.

stem: Over 1926–2016 (U.S. data in the textbook) small-company stocks averaged 16.6% per year, large-company stocks 12.0% and Treasury bills 3.4%. What was the average risk premium on small-company stocks?
explanation: Small-company premium = 16.6% − 3.4% = 13.2%. The 16.6% is the whole return; 8.6% is the large-company premium (12.0 − 3.4); 4.6% is the difference between the two stock classes (16.6 − 12.0), not a premium over T-bills.

stem: Why do risk-averse investors demand a positive risk premium on stocks?
options: Because they could hold the risk-free asset instead, so a risky asset must be expected to pay more.
Because stocks are guaranteed to beat T-bills in every year, so the premium is certain.
Because the government requires issuers to pay a premium over T-bills.
Because the standard deviation of stocks is always lower than that of T-bills.
explanation: The risk premium is compensation: people want to be paid for taking on risk. It is an expected (average) reward, not a guarantee in any single year.

stem: Using six years of data, the average observed risk premium on large-company stocks was −1.51% per annum. Does this show that investors are not risk averse?
options: Yes. A negative average premium proves that investors accept less than the risk-free rate for bearing risk.
Yes. A negative premium means the stock has become risk free relative to Treasury bills.
No. A premium can never be negative by definition, so the six-year data must contain an error.
No. Expected premiums are positive, but realized premiums can be negative when stock returns come in low or T-bill returns come in high.
explanation: Risk aversion is about what investors require ex ante. Ex post, a short sample can easily produce a negative realized premium; this does not change the required premium going forward.

stem: Which of the following is NOT another name for the risk premium?
options: the risk-free rate
the excess return
the equity risk premium (when the risky asset is the stock market)
the reward for bearing risk
explanation: The risk-free rate R_F is the base that is subtracted. The risk premium E[R] − R_F is also called the excess return.

stem: An investor who is neutral toward risk needs no compensation for it: she would accept the same expected return on a risky asset as on T-bills.
options: True
False
explanation: True. The lecture's three attitudes are averse, neutral and seeking. Being neutral toward risk means no compensation is needed for risk, so only the expected return matters, not the standard deviation.

stem: The risk premium is also called the _____ return.
options: nominal
real
excess
geometric
explanation: The professor uses 'risk premium' and 'excess return' interchangeably: the return above the risk-free rate, E[R] − R_F.

stem: Which ordering of long-run average annual returns (highest first) matches the U.S. record from 1926 to 2016?
options: large-company stocks, small-company stocks, Treasury bills, long-term bonds
long-term bonds, large-company stocks, small-company stocks, Treasury bills
small-company stocks, large-company stocks, long-term bonds, Treasury bills
Treasury bills, long-term bonds, large-company stocks, small-company stocks
explanation: Averages were roughly 16.6% for small stocks, 12.0% for large stocks, 6.0-6.3% for long-term bonds and 3.4% for T-bills: stocks beat bonds beat bills, and small beat large.

stem: Which observation best illustrates the first lesson of capital market history, that risky assets on average earn a risk premium?
options: Large-company stocks averaged about 8.6 percentage points more per year than Treasury bills.
Treasury bills had the highest standard deviation of all asset classes.
Inflation averaged about 3.0% per year over the same 1926-2016 period.
Long-term corporate bonds outperformed small-company stocks.
explanation: A positive average gap between a risky asset (large stocks, 12.0%) and the risk-free asset (T-bills, 3.4%) is the reward for bearing risk. The other options are false or unrelated to the premium.

stem: How do the first and second lessons of capital market history differ?
options: First: the greater the reward, the greater the risk. Second: risky assets earn a premium on average.
First: bonds beat stocks on average. Second: stocks then beat bills in the long run.
First: returns are normally distributed. Second: returns are independent of risk.
First: risky assets earn a premium on average. Second: greater potential reward comes with greater risk.
explanation: The first lesson is about the average reward for bearing risk; the second links the size of that reward to the size of the risk, measured by standard deviation: small stocks (σ about 31.9%) paid most and were most volatile.

stem: Over 1926-2016 (U.S. data in the textbook) small-company stocks averaged 16.6% per year against 12.0% for large-company stocks. Why doesn't everyone simply buy small-company stocks?
options: Because small-company stocks have a negative risk premium over T-bills.
Because their returns are far more volatile: σ about 31.9% versus 19.9%.
Because small-company stocks have a lower standard deviation than T-bills.
Because large-company stocks have always outperformed them in every year.
explanation: Higher average return comes with higher volatility, the second lesson of history. The extra return is the compensation for that risk.

stem: In a year when Treasury bills returned 7.7% and inflation was 6.2%, what was the real return on Treasury bills, in % per annum? Use the Fisher relationship.

errors.label: Subtracted inflation from the nominal rate
errors.explain: That shortcut ignores that inflation also erodes the return itself; the Fisher relationship divides the growth factors.

errors.label: Divided the factors upside down
errors.explain: Real purchasing-power growth is (1 + R_nom)/(1 + R_inf), nominal over inflation.

explanation: Fisher: (1 + R_real) = (1 + R_nom)/(1 + R_inf) = 1.077/1.062 = 1.0141, so the real return is about 1.41%, a little less than the simple 1.5% difference.

stem: A pension fund wants a real return of 4.0% per annum when inflation is expected to be 2.5% per annum. What nominal return does it need, in % per annum?

errors.label: Added real return and inflation
errors.explain: Adding ignores the cross term: the extra purchasing power must itself be inflated (0.04 × 0.025 = 0.1%).

errors.label: Divided instead of multiplying
errors.explain: To go from real to nominal you multiply the growth factors; dividing goes from nominal to real.

explanation: Fisher: (1 + R_nom) = (1 + R_inf)(1 + R_real) = 1.025 × 1.04 = 1.066, so the fund needs 6.60% nominal.

stem: From 1926 to 2016 (U.S. data in the textbook) small-company stocks averaged a nominal 16.6% per year while inflation averaged 3.0% per year. What was the average real return on small-company stocks, in % per annum?

errors.label: Subtracted inflation from the nominal return
errors.explain: The back-of-envelope 13.6% overstates the real return; the Fisher relationship gives 13.20%.

errors.label: Multiplied by the inflation factor
errors.explain: Real returns come from dividing by the inflation factor, not multiplying.

explanation: Real return = 1.166/1.03 − 1 = 13.20%; the textbook's quick estimate 16.6% − 3.0% = 13.6% is only an approximation.

stem: A Canadian equity fund earned a nominal 9.0% in a year when inflation was 2.4%. What was its real return?
explanation: Real return = 1.090/1.024 − 1 = 6.45%. Simple subtraction gives 6.60% (ignores compounding of inflation), multiplying the factors gives 11.62% (that is how you would go from real to nominal), and 2.4 − 9.0 = −6.60% is the wrong order.

stem: Because Treasury bills averaged 3.4% and inflation 3.0% over 1926-2016 (U.S. data in the textbook), the average real return on T-bills was only about 0.4% per year.
options: True
False
explanation: True. T-bills barely kept pace with inflation: 1.034/1.030 − 1 ≈ 0.39%. They had little default risk but still carried inflation risk.

stem: In one year large-company stocks lost 12% while T-bills gained 3%. Does this contradict the first lesson of capital market history?
options: No. The first lesson is about long-run average premiums; in any single year a large loss is still possible.
Yes. If stocks carry a premium they must beat T-bills in every single year, without exception.
Yes. A single losing year is enough to show that stocks carry no premium at all.
No. Stocks that lose in one year are guaranteed to recover the whole loss within the next year.
explanation: Risk premiums are averages. Individual years can be far below T-bills, which is precisely what volatility (standard deviation) measures.

stem: Which statement is NOT supported by the historical record for 1926-2016 in the textbook?
options: Treasury bills were more volatile than small-company stocks.
Small-company stocks had the highest standard deviation of the asset classes shown.
Treasury bills earned only slightly more than inflation on average.
Large-company stocks earned a positive average premium over Treasury bills.
explanation: Standard deviations: T-bills about 3.1% versus small-company stocks about 31.9%. Higher average returns came with higher volatility, not the reverse.

stem: Treasury bills are usually called risk free. In what sense can they still be risky for an investor?
options: Inflation can exceed their return, so purchasing power can fall even though the nominal return is positive.
They have a high probability of default because governments often fail to repay.
Their prices swing more than stock prices do because of their very long maturity.
They carry the same standard deviation as small-company stocks, about 31.9% per year.
explanation: T-bills have very little default risk and, being short term, little interest rate risk. The remaining risk is inflation risk: a nominal return of 7% is a loss in purchasing power when inflation is 9%.

stem: Which equation links the nominal return, the inflation rate and the real return?
options: R_real = R_nom − R_inf exactly
(1 + R_nom) = (1 + R_inf) + (1 + R_real)
R_nom = R_real ÷ R_inf
(1 + R_nom) = (1 + R_inf)(1 + R_real)
explanation: The Fisher relationship multiplies growth factors. R_nom − R_inf is only a close approximation when rates are small.
